newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 13.

text.p: Increased government spending under a coalition administration was inevitable, NZ First leader Winston Peters said on Tuesday. Spending would have to increase because of NZ First's commitment to addressing crises in health, education, law and order, and the export sector, Peters said. NZ First's economic policy estimated its policies would cost $1.6 billion a year more than present National Government policies. Peters said he thought there was "a certain inevitability" that the Reserve Bank's 0-2 percent inflation target would be widened by a coalition government. Page 1.

The Alliance on Tuesday followed up its pre-election promises to raise the minimum wage by launching a campaign called "All I want for Christmas is $300 a week". The caretaker government is required to review the minimum wage levels before December 31 and the Alliance wants the minimum adult rate to be lifted to $7.50 an hour from $6.375. Page 2.

List MPs are frustrated that they are not allowed to draw on the same electorate allowances as their constituency colleagues. Most political parties plan to use the list MPs to represent targeted areas, requiring them to set up electorate offices. However, list MPs say they cannot perform their new duties properly when they are eligible for only a portion of the allowances that constituency MPs receive. Page 2.

The Council of Trade Unions wants Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash sacked for his latest comments about the economy and his warning that increased spending might mean next year's tax cuts have to be delayed. "He has made it impossible for any incoming government to keep him on and maintain his own credibility," CTU president Ken Douglas said. Page 2.

Anchor spreadable butter is to be made in Europe, but not from New Zealand butter. The European-made butter is to be sold in packaging identical to the normal supply of Anchor Butter, but without the words "Produce of New Zealand". The switch
follows an increase in tariffs on exports of spreadable butter after new European Union regulations meant it could not be treated as normal butter. Page 3

Sealord's Nelson fish processing plant has been barred from exporting to the European Union and North American markets by Agriculture Ministry officials. Sealord, the biggest fishing firm in New Zealand with a $300 million turnover, said the suspension was not over food safety, but over factory processes and systems. About 60 percent of the Nelson plant's production usually went to the Union and North American markets. The plant could still supply fish to New Zealand, Australian and Asian markets despite the ban. Page 20.

Electricity supply companies will receive their first power bills on Wednesday under the new wholesale market rules, with thousands of pages of supporting documentation. The documentation from market operator EMCO is to show that the supply companies actually took the power they are being charged for - though EMCO says the bills will have to be adjusted, apparently because of a foul-up from grid operator Trans Power. Page 20.

The first month's prices for the new wholesale electricity market, issued on Tuesday by EMCO, show North Island prices rose during October while South Island prices fell. The North Island average price for the month was 4.4 cents a kilowatt-hour and for the South Island the average price was 3.2 cents a kilowatt-hour. Page 20.

Costs associated with the acquisition of Trust Bank by Westpac trimmed $43.5 million off the combined banks' bottom line for the year to September, Westpac New Zealand chief executive Harry Price said on Tuesday. Westpac New Zealand operations showed a profit after tax of $127.3 million for the September year. Trust Bank was acquired early this year. Page 20.

Continuing but lower economic growth and a flat savings ratio were confirmed by national accounts issued on Tuesday by Statistics New Zealand. The data showed gross domestic product rose by six percent to $91.04 billion in the year to March 1996, compared with 6.9 percent in 1995's period. Page 21.

Manufactuers already holding costs 15 percent below those in Australia need fiscal restraint by the new government if they are to remain competitive, according to the Manufacturers Federation. Page 26.
